problems.title: A minimum needs a restriction on the addends
problems.question: Split 48 into two addends so that the cube of the first plus the square of the second is smallest.
problems.idea: State the domain: real unrestricted addends have no minimum.
formulas: Let the cubed addend be t, so F=t³+(48-t)²; F′=3t²+2t-96=(t+6)(3t-16).
steps: If t is unrestricted, F→-∞ as t→-∞, so no smallest value exists.
If nonnegative addends are intended, 0≤t≤48. The derivative changes from negative to positive at t=16/3, giving the minimum there.
The other addend is 48-16/3=128/3. If positive integers are intended instead, compare t=5,6 and the endpoints; t=5,43 gives 1974 versus 1980 at 6,42.
problems.answer: Unrestricted real addends: no minimum. Nonnegative real addends: 16/3 and 128/3. Positive integer addends: 5 and 43.
problems.note: The printed question does not specify nonnegative or integer addends. Different domains genuinely give different answers.

problems.title: An integrable vertical endpoint
problems.question: Find the area bounded by x=-1,x=0,y=0 and $y=x^2+e^x+1/\sqrt{1-x^2}$.
problems.idea: All terms are positive; the endpoint singularity needs an improper integral.
steps: Integrate from -1+ε to 0 and then let ε→0⁺.
The polynomial part gives 1/3, the exponential part gives 1-e⁻¹, and arcsine gives π/2.
All three limits are finite, so the area is their sum.

problems.title: Concavity can change at a vertical tangent
problems.question: Find the concavity intervals and inflection points of $y=\sqrt[3]{x+1}-\sqrt[3]{x-1}$.
problems.idea: Use real cube roots, including for negative inputs.
steps: For x<-1 the bracket is negative, so y″>0. For -1<x<1 it is positive, so y″<0. For x>1 it is negative again, so y″>0.
The function is continuous at ±1, although its derivative is unbounded there.
Concavity changes at both points. Their y-coordinates are both ∛2.
problems.answer: Concave up: (-∞,-1),(1,∞). Concave down: (-1,1). Inflection points: (-1,∛2),(1,∛2).
problems.note: These inflections have vertical tangents. A definition requiring a finite derivative would exclude them; the usual definition by continuity and concavity change includes both.

problems.title: Build the rational graph from its features
problems.question: Sketch $y=2x^3/(x^2-4)$.
problems.idea: Find asymptotes, turning points and curvature; use odd symmetry.
steps: The domain excludes ±2. The graph is odd and passes through (0,0); vertical asymptotes are x=±2 and the slant asymptote is y=2x.
It increases on (-∞,-2√3),(2√3,∞), and decreases on (-2√3,-2),(-2,2),(2,2√3). The stationary point at 0 does not reverse monotonicity.
The local maximum is (-2√3,-6√3); the local minimum is (2√3,6√3). The origin is a stationary inflection.
It is concave down on (-∞,-2),(0,2), concave up on (-2,0),(2,∞). At -2 the left/right limits are -∞,+∞; at 2 they are -∞,+∞.
problems.answer: Three branches with vertical asymptotes x=±2, slant asymptote y=2x, turning points (±2√3,±6√3), and an inflection at (0,0).

problems.title: Two frusta fit the same diagonal data
problems.question: A cone frustum’s axial diagonals have length 3 m, cross in ratio 2:1, and form an angle of 120°. Find its volume and lateral area.
problems.idea: The ratio fixes R=2r, but the unoriented diagonal angle permits two shapes.
steps: Since R/r=2, write R+r=3r. The squared horizontal and vertical components are 27/4 and 9/4 in either order.
Case 1: r=√3/2,R=√3,h=3/2. The slant is √3, giving V=21π/8 m³ and S=9π/2 m².
Case 2: r=1/2,R=1,h=3√3/2. The slant is √7, giving V=7π√3/8 m³ and S=3π√7/2 m².
In each case one pair of angles at the diagonal crossing is 120° and the other is 60°. Both meet the stated data.
problems.answer: Two possibilities: (V,S)=(21π/8,9π/2) or (7π√3/8,3π√7/2), in m³ and m².
problems.note: To select one frustum, the question must specify which angle is 120°, such as the angle facing a base. A plain angle “between the diagonals” does not select it.

problems.title: A circle tangent to a given line
problems.question: Find the circle with centre (6,7) tangent to 5x-12y-24=0.
problems.idea: Its radius is the perpendicular distance to the line.
steps: The numerator is |30-84-24|=78 and the normal length is 13.
Thus r=6, giving the required equation.

problems.title: A logarithm base above or below one
problems.question: Solve $\log_{|x|}(\sqrt{9-x^2}-x-1)\ge1$.
formulas: For b>1, log_bA≥1 iff A≥b; for 0<b<1, log_bA≥1 iff 0<A≤b.
steps: Start with -3≤x≤3 and x≠-1,0,1. If x<-1, A≥-x simplifies to √(9-x²)≥1, giving -2√2≤x<-1.
If x>1, A≥x would require √(9-x²)≥2x+1. Squaring gives 5x²+4x-8≤0, impossible for x>1.
For -1<x<0, A≤-x would require √(9-x²)≤1, impossible there.
For 0<x<1, A>0 automatically and A≤x gives √(9-x²)≤2x+1, hence 5x²+4x-8≥0. Thus x≥(-2+2√11)/5.

problems.title: Largest cone in a sphere
problems.question: A cone of greatest volume is inscribed in a sphere of radius R. Find the ratio of cone height to R.
problems.idea: Express its base radius in terms of height.
steps: For 0≤h≤2R, differentiate: V′=(π/3)h(4R-3h).
The interior maximum is h=4R/3; endpoint volumes are zero.
Thus the cone height is 4/3 times the sphere radius.

problems.title: The logarithms eliminate a spurious circle intersection
problems.question: Solve $x^2+y^2=4+y/2$, $\log_3(x+2y)+\log_{1/3}(x-2y)=1$.
problems.idea: Combine the logarithms only after recording both positive arguments.
steps: The second equation gives x+2y=3(x-2y), hence x=4y. The positive arguments then require y>0.
Substitute into the first equation: 34y²-y-8=0, with roots y=1/2 and y=-8/17.
Only the positive root is valid; x=4y=2.

problems.title: Two logarithmic roots with the same sign
problems.question: Find all a for which $(a-2)^2 2^x-(a-1)2^{-x}+2a-5=0$ has two distinct roots x of the same sign.
problems.idea: Set t=2ˣ. Same-sign negative x means both t-roots lie between 0 and 1.
formulas: After multiplication by t: Q(t)=(a-2)²t²+(2a-5)t+1-a; Δ=4a³-16a²+12a+9.
steps: Two positive t-roots require a<1 by their product; the sum is then positive. At a=2 the equation is linear and cannot have two roots.
To place both roots on the same side of 1, need Q(1)=a(a-3)>0. Combined with a<1 this gives a<0.
For a<0, the vertex t₀=(5-2a)/[2(a-2)²] lies in (0,1). Thus Δ>0 and Q(1)>0 place both roots in (0,1); both x-roots are negative.
On a<0 the discriminant polynomial is strictly increasing, because its derivative 12a²-32a+12>0. It has exactly one negative zero α≈-0.44985. Hence Δ>0 precisely for α<a<0 in this range.
problems.answer: α<a<0, where α is the unique negative root of 4α³-16α²+12α+9=0 (α≈-0.44985).
problems.note: The endpoints are excluded: at α the two roots merge; at a=0 one root is x=0, which has no positive or negative sign.
